# Code review iteration

Reviewed the full source of `github.com/kamilsk/semaphore/v5` at commit `91c10c6 2020-04-16`: all seven Go files (`semaphore.go`, `interface.go`, `default.go`, `draft.go` plus the three test files), `go.mod`/`go.sum`, `Makefile`, `.travis.yml`, and `README.md`. Review angle: correctness of the semaphore semantics, cancellation handling, API guarantees, and how the 2020-era decisions hold up in the Go 1.26 ecosystem. `.github/reviews/` did not exist, so there are no previous review files to match against; `.github/issues/` and `.github/roadmap/` were ignored as offline backlog dumps.

Severity: **Crit** / **High** / **Med** / **Low** / **Nit**.
Class: `correctness` · `security` · `concurrency` · `perf` · `api` · `idiom` · `modern` · `test` · `build` · `docs`.

## 1. Double call of a ReleaseFunc silently frees a slot it does not own

Anchor: semaphore.go:47-53 together with semaphore.go:11-15.

```go
case semaphore <- struct{}{}:
	return func() { _ = semaphore.Release() }, nil //nolint: gas
```

The `ReleaseFunc` returned by a successful `Acquire`/`Catch` is not idempotent: every invocation performs one `<-semaphore` receive. The classic calling pattern — release early on one path while also having `defer release()` — pops **two** tokens for a single acquisition. The second pop frees a slot owned by some other goroutine, so `Occupied()` under-reports and the semaphore starts admitting more concurrent holders than its capacity. This is exactly the failure mode a semaphore exists to prevent, and it is silent: `ReleaseFunc.Release` (semaphore.go:12-15) is hard-coded to `f(); return nil`, discarding the `errEmpty` that the inner `Release` would have surfaced when the count finally bottoms out. `golang.org/x/sync/semaphore` panics on over-release for precisely this reason — silent miscounting is far worse than a crash.

**Fix.** Make the returned closure idempotent (guard it with a `sync.Once`, or nil-out captured state), and stop swallowing the error: either propagate `errEmpty` through `ReleaseFunc.Release` or panic with a descriptive message on over-release. Add a regression test that calls the release func twice and asserts `Occupied()` stays consistent.

## 2. Signal can leak an acquired slot and a goroutine forever

Anchor: semaphore.go:82-91.

```go
ch := make(chan ReleaseFunc, 1)
go func() {
	if release, err := semaphore.Acquire(deadline); err == nil {
		ch <- release
	}
	close(ch)
}()
```

Two independent leak modes. First, the channel is buffered, so when `Acquire` succeeds after the caller has stopped listening — the natural outcome when `Signal(ctx.Done())` is used inside a `select` against other events — the `ReleaseFunc` is parked in the buffer and the acquired slot is occupied forever. The semaphore permanently loses capacity with no way to detect or recover it. Second, with a `nil` (or never-closed) deadline while the semaphore stays full, the inner `Acquire` blocks forever and the goroutine leaks. Both failures are invisible to the caller, and the same `Signal(Breaker) <-chan Releaser` shape is carried forward into the v5 `Interface` (interface.go:34), so the design flaw propagates into the new API.

**Fix.** Use an unbuffered channel and race the handoff against the deadline: after a successful acquire, `select { case ch <- release: case <-deadline: release() }` before `close(ch)`, so an abandoned signal returns its slot. Document that a `nil` deadline can pin a goroutine — or reconsider whether `Signal` belongs in the API at all; in modern Go the caller can trivially wrap `Acquire` in a goroutine themselves.

## 3. Toolchain, CI, and dependencies are frozen in 2020

Anchor: go.mod:3, .travis.yml:1-40, Makefile:124-135, README.md:107-118.

The repository has effectively had **no CI since 2021**: `.travis.yml` targets travis-ci.org, which shut down, so the build matrix (Go master, 1.7–1.13) and the build badge are dead. The rest of the stack is equally stale: `go 1.11` directive with no `toolchain` line (Go 1.26 is current; 1.11 predates `errors.Is`, generics, fuzzing, `t.Setenv`, `-shuffle`); `testify v1.3.0` (January 2019) pulled in — and vendored — for a single `assert.True` call; a committed `vendor/` tree plus `GOFLAGS=-mod=vendor`, which the module proxy and sumdb made pointless for a zero-dependency library; README badges pointing at godoc.org (sunset in favor of pkg.go.dev) and cdn.rawgit.com (service shut down in 2019, so the "awesome" badge is a broken image); installation instructions built around `dep` (archived in 2020) and GOPATH; a `//nolint: gas` directive for a linter that was renamed to `gosec` in 2018 and a nolint syntax golangci-lint no longer accepts (no space, reason required); Makefile helpers for Go 1.11–1.14 Docker images and a 1-second test timeout that will flake on any loaded runner. There is no govulncheck, no Dependabot, no GitHub Actions.

**Fix.** Migration outline: (1) delete `.travis.yml`; add `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with `actions/checkout` + `actions/setup-go` on a `stable`/`oldstable` matrix running `go test -race -shuffle=on ./...`, `golangci-lint`, and `govulncheck ./...`; (2) `go mod edit -go=1.25` (or current oldstable), drop testify in favor of the stdlib (one assertion), delete `vendor/` and the `-mod=vendor` flags, `go mod tidy`; (3) add `.github/dependabot.yml` covering `gomod` and `github-actions`; (4) refresh README: pkg.go.dev badge, GitHub Actions badge, delete the dep/GOPATH/rawgit material and the stale golang/go wiki links.

## 4. Anyone can call Release without owning a slot

Anchor: semaphore.go:73-80; also interface.go:42-44, interface.go:29-30, default.go:25-27.

```go
func (semaphore semaphore) Release() error {
	select {
	case <-semaphore:
		return nil
	...
```

Release capability is ambient: `Semaphore` embeds `Releaser`, and `default.go` even exports a package-level `Release()`. Any code — including code that never acquired — can free a slot belonging to another holder, and the call only errors when the semaphore is already completely empty. Worse, the API offers two parallel release mechanisms (the semaphore-level `Release` and the per-acquisition `ReleaseFunc`), and mixing them produces exactly the double-free of finding 1. The README quick start (README.md:45) models the semaphore-level style, steering users toward the fragile variant. The v5 `Interface` (interface.go:29-30) still embeds `Releaser`, so the trap survives the redesign.

**Fix.** Make the `Releaser` returned by `Acquire`/`Try` the *only* way to release: drop `Release` from `Semaphore`, from the planned `Interface`, and from the package-level default API in v5. This turns "who may release" from a convention into a capability enforced by the type system.

## 5. Error API predates errors.Is and misreports cancellation as timeout

Anchor: semaphore.go:37-43 and semaphore.go:22-35.

```go
errTimeout = errors.New("operation timeout")
...
func IsTimeout(err error) bool { return err == errTimeout }
```

Two problems. First, the sentinels are unexported and matched with `==` through bespoke `IsEmpty`/`IsNoPlace`/`IsTimeout` helpers — a pre-Go-1.13 pattern. The moment a caller wraps the error (`fmt.Errorf("acquire: %w", err)`), all three helpers return false, and callers cannot use `errors.Is` themselves because the sentinels are private. Second, the semantics lie: `Acquire` returns `errTimeout` whenever the deadline channel closes, but that channel frequently closes due to explicit cancellation (`context.WithCancel`, `breaker.BreakByContext`), not a timeout. Logs and metrics keyed on "operation timeout" will misclassify plain cancellations.

**Fix.** Export the sentinels (`ErrEmpty`, `ErrNoPlace`, and a more honest `ErrCanceled` or `ErrBreak`), keep the `Is*` helpers as thin `errors.Is` wrappers for compatibility, and delete the `==` comparisons. Longer term, accept a `context.Context` in the v5 API and return `context.Cause(ctx)` so callers can distinguish `context.DeadlineExceeded` from `context.Canceled` the standard way.

## 6. Unfinished draft ships in the release and does not implement Interface

Anchor: draft.go:10-38, interface.go:37, draft_test.go:1.

```go
func (semaphore *draft) Release() error {
	panic("implement me")
}
```

`draft.go` is scaffolding — four of six methods are `panic("implement me")` — yet it is compiled into the tagged v5 release candidate of a public library. It is also demonstrably unchecked: `Interface` declares `Size(uint) uint32` (interface.go:37) while the draft implements `Size(new uint32) uint32`, so `*draft` does not even satisfy the interface it drafts; a `var _ Interface = (*draft)(nil)` assertion would have caught this at compile time. The parts that are implemented have their own defects: `Size` is a non-atomic load-then-store read-modify-write, so two concurrent `Size(n)` calls race and one capacity update is lost, and the parameter `new` shadows the builtin. `draft_test.go` contains only the package clause. As an audit of past decisions: parking aspirational API in the release branch is why the README documents an API that panics (finding 7).

**Fix.** Delete `draft.go` and `draft_test.go` from the release branch and develop the v5 `Interface` implementation on a feature branch. When it returns, add compile-time interface assertions, reconcile the `uint`/`uint32` inconsistency (pick `int`, matching the stdlib and `x/sync/semaphore`), and guard capacity mutation with a CAS loop or mutex.

## 7. README examples do not compile against the shipped API

Anchor: README.md:15-21 and README.md:33-51.

```go
if _, err := limiter.Acquire(
	breaker.BreakByContext(
		context.WithTimeout(req.Context(), time.Second),
	),
); err != nil {
```

Both front-page examples pass a `breaker.Breaker` value to `Acquire`, but every `Acquire` in this module — package-level (default.go:10) and method (semaphore.go:47) — takes a `<-chan struct{}`. `breaker.BreakByTimeout(...)` / `breaker.BreakByContext(...)` return interface values, not channels, so neither snippet compiles; they document the aspirational v5 `Interface`, whose only implementation is the panicking draft (finding 6). Anyone evaluating the library by copying the quick start hits compile errors immediately — the worst possible first impression for a returning open-source project.

**Fix.** Rewrite the examples against the shipped API (`limiter.Acquire(ctx.Done())` or `breaker.BreakByTimeout(time.Second).Done()`), and encode them as testable `Example` functions in an `example_test.go` so CI keeps the README-adjacent code honest permanently.

## 8. Default semaphore capacity is frozen at init and shared process-wide

Anchor: default.go:5.

```go
var def = New(runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0))
```

Two distinct problems. First, capacity is captured once at package initialization. Anything that adjusts `GOMAXPROCS` afterwards — `automaxprocs`, manual tuning, and since Go 1.25 the runtime itself, which now tracks container CPU limits dynamically — leaves the default semaphore sized for a stale value. In 2026 this decision ages worse than it did in 2020, because `GOMAXPROCS` is no longer a boot-time constant. Second, `def` is a single hidden global shared by *every* importer in the process: two unrelated dependencies that both call `semaphore.Acquire(...)` silently contend for the same `GOMAXPROCS` slots — invisible cross-library coupling, aggravated by the package-level `Release()` (finding 4) which lets one library free the other's slots. Nothing in the docs states the default capacity or the sharing.

**Fix.** Drop the package-level default instance and its function mirrors in v5 — a semaphore is cheap to construct and callers should own their instances. If a default must stay for compatibility, document its capacity and process-wide sharing explicitly and consider sizing it lazily.

## 9. Package-level tests are order-dependent and TestSignal leaks a slot

Anchor: default_test.go:54-58; also default_test.go:21-33, semaphore_test.go:15-32.

```go
func TestSignal(t *testing.T) {
	if release, ok := <-Signal(nil); release == nil || !ok {
		t.Error("unexpected signal")
	}
}
```

`TestSignal` acquires a slot from the shared package-level `def` and never calls the received release func, permanently leaking one slot of the default semaphore for the rest of the test binary. The suite only passes because Go executes tests in source order and `TestOccupied` (which asserts `Occupied() == 0`) happens to run first; `go test -shuffle=on` — a flag that has existed since Go 1.17 and belongs in any modern CI invocation — breaks the package. Additional weaknesses: `TestAcquire` relies on 10ms wall-clock deadlines (flaky under load, especially with the Makefile's 1s global timeout), and `TestSemaphore_Acquire_Timeout` iterates a test table without `t.Run`, so a failure cannot be attributed to a case. Testify is imported for exactly one assertion (semaphore_test.go:30).

**Fix.** Call the received release func in `TestSignal`; stop asserting against shared mutable package state (construct fresh semaphores, or reset/skip the default-instance tests); wrap table cases in `t.Run(tc.name, ...)`; enable `-shuffle=on -race` in CI; replace the lone testify assertion with stdlib checks and drop the dependency.

## 10. New panics on negative capacity and yields a dead semaphore for zero

Anchor: semaphore.go:18-20.

```go
func New(capacity int) Semaphore {
	return make(semaphore, capacity)
}
```

`New(-1)` panics at runtime with the implementation-leaking `makechan: size out of range` instead of a message that names the package and the misuse. `New(0)` is accepted and produces a semaphore whose `Acquire` can never succeed — the tests exploit this deliberately as a fixture, but for a public constructor it is an undocumented foot-gun: a capacity computed at runtime that collapses to zero turns every acquire site into a guaranteed timeout with no hint why.

**Fix.** Validate the argument: panic with a descriptive `semaphore: capacity must be positive`-style message (matching how `sync` primitives report misuse), or return an error. Document the zero-capacity behavior explicitly if it is meant to stay as a "closed" semaphore idiom.

## 11. Acquire outcome is random when the deadline is already expired

Anchor: semaphore.go:47-53.

When the deadline channel is already closed *and* a slot is free, both `select` cases are ready and the runtime picks pseudo-randomly: `Acquire` may succeed even though the caller's deadline has long passed (in the README's HTTP scenario, the handler proceeds to do work for a request whose context is dead), or it may return `errTimeout` despite free capacity. `x/sync/semaphore` exhibits and *documents* the same relaxation; here it is completely unspecified, so callers cannot know whether checking `ctx.Err()` after a successful acquire is their job.

**Fix.** If expiry should dominate, add a non-blocking priority check before the main select (`select { case <-deadline: return nothing, errTimeout; default: }`). Otherwise, keep the behavior and document the nondeterminism on `Acquire`, as the stdlib does.
